The Pouched lamprey Geotria australis emerges from the fertilised ovum as a minute larva, its initial wet body mass at the completion of yolk-sac resorption being remarkably low at only 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams]. This minuscule size at the onset of exogenous feeding is a direct consequence of the extremely small diameter of the ovum, which measures approximately one millimetre. Following this trophic switch, the ammocoete larva enters an extended period of filter-feeding and gradual somatic growth in the soft sediments of freshwater streams. During this larval phase, which can persist for several years, the animal accumulates substantial body mass before the radical metamorphosis that transforms it into a free-swimming juvenile. Field records indicate that individuals attaining the larval stage where metamorphosis is initiated are still quite modest in size, typically measuring only a few centimetres in total body length. The species is known for its complex life cycle, which includes a prolonged freshwater residency followed by a marine phase as a sexually maturing adult.

As individuals undergo metamorphosis and transition into the juvenile stage, body size increases steadily. The total length at which puberty is reached, marking the onset of gonadal maturation, has been recorded at 10.1 centimetres [Lp = 10.1 centimetres]. This measurement was derived from dissections of specimens captured during their upstream spawning migration and represents a consistent threshold across several studied populations. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is correspondingly modest, with individuals at this developmental milestone averaging approximately 1.23 grams [Wwp = approximately 1.23 grams]. This relatively small mass at the initiation of reproductive development indicates that a substantial portion of the species' somatic growth occurs after sexual maturity has been attained. The disparity between the size at puberty and the much larger dimensions achieved later in life underscores the lamprey's capacity for continued growth during the marine feeding phase. The onset of reproductive activation at this length is typical among Southern Hemisphere lampreys, although intraspecific variation is observed in response to local stream productivity and thermal regimes. Further work is needed to clarify how these size thresholds relate to the timing of the seaward migration.

The ultimate total length attained by Geotria australis is considerable for a lamprey, with the longest documented individuals reaching 57 centimetres [Li = 57 centimetres] from the oral disc to the tip of the tail. This maximum recorded size, obtained from the largest specimens captured in commercial and research nets off the coasts of southern South America and Australia, places the species among the more elongated members of its family. Corresponding to this substantial length, the ultimate wet weight for these largest individuals has been calculated at approximately 222 grams [Wwi = approximately 222 grams], reflecting a robust body composition acquired during the marine phase when they feed parasitically on large teleost fish. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a cubic scaling law typical of fusiform fishes. These maximum dimensions are attained only after several years of active feeding in the ocean, following the completion of the larval stage and metamorphosis. The dramatic increase in mass from the 1.23 gram [Wwp = 1.23 gram] weight at puberty to the 222 gram ultimate weight represents a more than 180-fold gain, highlighting the extraordinarily productive feeding conditions encountered in the marine environment.

Fecundity in Geotria australis is influenced strongly by the thermal conditions experienced during ovarian development. Under a controlled experimental temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], dissections of gravid females approaching the end of their life cycle have revealed a mean fecundity of 68,212 eggs . This high egg number is necessary given the extremely small size of the fertilised ova and the presumed low survival rate of the larvae in the challenging stream environment. The total reproductive output essentially represents the entirety of the female's remaining energy reserves, as lampreys are semelparous and die shortly after spawning. The time since birth at which puberty is attained under these same thermal conditions, also measured at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], has been established at approximately 1,278 days [tp = approximately 1,278 days], which equates to roughly three and a half years. This comparatively delayed onset of reproductive maturity is a hallmark of the species' life-history strategy, which prioritises a lengthy larval growth phase to accumulate sufficient resources for the subsequent metamorphosis and marine feeding excursion. The linkage between temperature and the pace of maturation is critical for understanding population dynamics.

The complete lifespan of Geotria australis, measured from the moment of syngamy to natural mortality following senescence after the single reproductive event, has been estimated at 9 years under the same controlled thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This value, which corresponds to approximately 3,285 days [am = approximately 3,285 days], encompasses the entire sequence from the zygote stage through larval development, metamorphosis, marine feeding, the upstream spawning migration, and eventual bi at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]ological death. The relatively long lifespan for such a small-bodied organism at birth is a consequence of the protracted larval phase, which can itself last for four to five years under natural stream conditions. Age-related death in this species typically occurs within a few weeks of spawning, as the adults cease feeding entirely during the upstream migration and progressively deteriorate due to the exhausting physiological demands of reproduction. Comparative analyses with other lamprey species, such as the Northern Hemisphere Petromyzon marinus, suggest that the pouched lamprey's lifespan is at the upper end of the range for the group. The post-reproductive mortality is absolute, with no individual surviving to spawn a second time. This semelparous life history strongly shapes the species' population biology and conservation requirements.
